stories.headline: TECH-LED RALLY LIFTS S&P 500 TO 7,722 AS FED MEETING OPENS, EARNINGS BLITZ LOOMS
stories.body: The S&P 500 added 0.59% to roughly 7,722 and the Nasdaq 100 rose about 1.05% toward the 29,500s, with a semiconductor-industry gauge up 3.4% on the session. The gains came as the two-day FOMC meeting opened and investors positioned ahead of Wednesday's Meta, Microsoft and Tesla reports and Thursday's Apple print.
stories.explain: Chip stocks led because they're the most direct read-through on AI capex: if Meta, Microsoft and the other hyperscalers keep spending at current levels, semiconductor makers are the suppliers who get paid first and most directly. A rally into a Fed decision also reflects positioning — traders buying risk now on the expectation of a non-event hold tomorrow, which means any surprise in Wednesday's statement or press conference would hit a market that's already priced in calm.

stories.headline: FED OPENS TWO-DAY MEETING WITH A HOLD PRICED IN AFTER SEPTEMBER'S HIKE TO 3.75%-4.00%
stories.body: The FOMC's October meeting runs through Wednesday, with a decision due at 2 p.m. ET; futures markets assign an overwhelming probability to a hold after the Fed's September 25-basis-point hike pushed the target range to 3.75%-4.00%. The 10-year Treasury yield ticked up to roughly 4.99% as the meeting opened, extending its climb toward the psychologically significant 5% level.
stories.explain: A hold doesn't mean the Fed is done moving — it means the committee wants another inflation and jobs cycle of data before deciding whether September's hike was enough. The 10-year keeps climbing anyway because long-end yields aren't set by the fed funds rate directly; they're set by the market's expectation of where short rates average out over the next decade, plus a term premium investors demand for the uncertainty of holding duration that long. Right now that term premium is rising faster than any actual hike expectation.

stories.headline: CRUDE EXTENDS SLIDE TOWARD $100 AS MIDDLE EAST DE-ESCALATION PROGRESSES
stories.body: WTI fell about 0.9% to roughly $99.95 a barrel, a second straight daily decline, as diplomatic progress on Iran continued to ease the geopolitical risk premium priced into crude. Brent eased in tandem, keeping energy-sensitive CPI components in focus with the Fed one day from its decision.
stories.explain: Oil prices carry two components: a fundamental supply-demand price and a risk premium for the chance that a disruption — a strait closure, a strike on infrastructure — removes barrels from the market overnight. When mediation headlines make that disruption look less likely, traders who were long oil as a hedge unwind those positions, and the premium comes out of the price even before any physical barrel changes hands. A sustained pullback here is disinflationary and gives the Fed more room to hold rather than hike further.

stories.headline: BOEING STUMBLES ON DELIVERY CUT AS CELESTICA JUMPS AHEAD OF A HEAVY EARNINGS WEEK
stories.body: Boeing shares fell after the planemaker trimmed its delivery target, while contract manufacturer Celestica jumped in premarket trading after beating estimates — a split verdict heading into a week where Meta, Microsoft and Tesla report Wednesday and Apple reports Thursday, with capital-expenditure guidance the number that matters most.
stories.explain: Capex guidance moves these stocks more than the quarter's actual revenue because the market is trying to answer one question across the whole sector: is AI spending still accelerating, or is it starting to plateau? A single capex number resets the earnings trajectory for every chip and data-center supplier downstream, which is why a beat-and-raise quarter can still sell off if the spending commentary disappoints, and why a modest miss with aggressive capex guidance — the pattern several hyperscalers have followed this year — keeps getting rewarded.

stories.headline: FORMER LOUISVILLE COACH KENNY PAYNE JOINS CALIPARI'S ARKANSAS STAFF AHEAD OF SEASON OPENER
stories.body: Arkansas added former Louisville head coach Kenny Payne to John Calipari's staff as the Razorbacks prepare for a season that tips off Nov. 2, days after Florida was tabbed the preseason No. 1 in the AP poll for the first time since 2006. The hire adds another head-coaching resume to Calipari's bench as he looks to rebound after an uneven first two seasons in Fayetteville.

stories.headline: NBA'S CLIPPERS CAP-CIRCUMVENTION PROBE TIED TO KAWHI LEONARD STAYS IN FOCUS
stories.body: The league's long-running review of the Clippers' defunct courtside-sponsorship arrangement and its ties to Kawhi Leonard remains active, with reports indicating the NBA continues examining whether the deal effectively circumvented the salary cap. Elsewhere, four games are on tonight's slate, including Detroit at New York, with the Pistons looking to open 3-0.

stories.headline: FALCONS CB JAMES PEARCE JR. SUSPENDED 8 GAMES FOR PERSONAL CONDUCT POLICY VIOLATION
stories.body: Atlanta cornerback James Pearce Jr. will miss eight games under the NFL's personal conduct policy, a significant blow to the Falcons' secondary. The suspension lands amid an already-active trade season — the Giants acquired QB J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings and the Steelers sent CB Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys — with the Nov. 10 trade deadline two weeks out.

stories.headline: PLAYOFF PICTURE TIGHTENS HEADING INTO WEEK 9 AS UNDEFEATEDS DWINDLE
stories.body: BYU's comeback win over Notre Dame two weeks ago is still reshaping the four-team playoff conversation, and this week's slate — including Washington's first-ever Big Ten meeting with Nebraska on Saturday — adds another data point before the committee's first rankings release. Few unbeaten teams remain nationally as rivalry week approaches.

deepDive.title: Why the 10-Year Keeps Climbing Even When the Fed Is About to Hold Steady
content: The Fed's October meeting opened today with markets all but certain tomorrow's decision will be a hold — no change from the 3.75%-4.00% range set by September's 25-basis-point hike. Yet the 10-year Treasury yield ticked up again today, to roughly 4.99%, continuing a climb that's been underway for weeks. To someone learning markets for the first time, that looks contradictory: if the Fed isn't moving, why is the most-watched yield in the world still rising? The answer is that the Fed Chair's gavel only directly controls one point on the curve, not the whole thing.

The FOMC sets the federal funds rate — the overnight rate banks charge each other for reserves — through tools like the interest rate on reserve balances and the reverse repo facility. That rate anchors the very short end of the yield curve almost mechanically. But the 10-year yield is a market price, set by millions of buy and sell decisions, and it reflects two separate things: the average level investors expect the fed funds rate to sit at over the next decade (the expectations component), plus a term premium — extra compensation investors demand for the risk that inflation or rates behave worse than expected over ten years instead of overnight.

What's easy to miss is that a rising 10-year with a steady Fed funds rate usually means the term premium is doing the moving, not the expectations component. That's exactly what happened in 1994's so-called "bond market massacre," when the Fed's tightening cycle was well-telegraphed but long yields still spiked more than short rates did, because investors repriced the uncertainty around how long elevated inflation would persist. Today's setup rhymes: the Fed holding at a still-elevated range signals it isn't confident inflation is fully tamed, and that uncertainty itself gets priced into the long end as extra compensation for duration risk.

For a market sitting at a 23-year rate high with earnings season running hot, this distinction matters more than Wednesday's statement will. If the Fed holds as priced and Powell's press conference offers no surprises, the bigger driver of where the 10-year goes next will be this week's Big Tech capex guidance and the inflation data that follows it — not anything said in the FOMC room. Watching the term premium, not just the headline fed funds decision, is the better way to read where borrowing costs are actually headed into year-end.
